# AI-Assisted Coding {#sec-ai-coding} ::: {.bookepigraph} ```{=latex} \begin{flushright}\small ``` *The real problem is not whether machines think but whether men do.* [B. F. Skinner]{.smallcaps}, *Contingencies of Reinforcement* (1969) ```{=latex} \end{flushright} ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Sources Blog posts `46-ellmerinRcoding` (ellmer package), `36-simpleshinyappwithchatgpt`; the `ellmer` package from Posit; direct experience with Claude Code during the development of this book. ::: ## Prerequisites Answer the following questions to see if you can bypass this chapter. You can find the answers at the end of the chapter in @sec-quiz-answers-21. 1. What does the `ellmer` R package provide that a browser-based chatbot does not? 2. What are three classes of bug that large language models routinely introduce into R code? 3. Why is it important to write the first draft of a non-trivial function without AI assistance before asking an LLM to refine it? ## Learning objectives By the end of this chapter you should be able to: - Use an LLM as a code-review assistant rather than a code generator. - Call an LLM programmatically from R with `ellmer`. - Set up Claude Code, ChatGPT, or a local LLM for terminal-based workflows. - Identify and avoid the LLM-specific failure modes that appear in R code (hallucinated APIs, silent type coercions, misuse of functions with confusing defaults). - Adopt the 'verify, then trust' workflow for every piece of AI-generated code. - Recognize when LLM assistance is net-helpful and when it is net-harmful. ## Orientation Large language models are now capable of producing working R code for the majority of the exercises in this book. This is a new fact, and one that deserves an explicit response. The position we take here is a simple one: **use LLMs as an amplifier, not a replacement**. Every line of generated code is to be treated as a hypothesis to be tested, and not as a result to be trusted. This chapter is the meta-chapter on the 'Collaborating with an LLM' callouts that appear throughout this book and its companion. It covers the tooling, the failure modes, and the workflow. ## The statistician's contribution {#sec-ai-coding-human} The skill is not getting code from an LLM; LLMs produce code easily. The skill is judging which code to trust, when, and why. **Reading is more valuable than writing now.** A generation ago, the bottleneck was producing code. Now, the bottleneck is reading produced code with sufficient care to spot the bugs. The biostatistician who can audit LLM-generated code quickly is the biostatistician who benefits from the LLM. **Domain knowledge is the moat.** An LLM cannot tell you whether to dichotomize a continuous outcome, whether to control for a baseline covariate, or whether to use a one-sided or two-sided test. These judgments depend on substantive understanding the LLM does not have. **Skepticism by default.** When the LLM produces a function that looks right, ask: how would I know if this were wrong? Run on adversarial inputs. Compare to a known-good reference. Read the source. The plausibility of the output is not the correctness of the output. **Document your prompt.** When the LLM produces something useful, save the prompt. The prompt is the specification; if you ever need to regenerate or revise the code, the prompt is the context. The 'Collaborating with an LLM' callouts in this book are exemplars: prompt, what to watch for, how to verify. These judgments are what distinguish AI assistance that produces correct, defensible code from AI assistance that produces working-looking but wrong code. ## The `ellmer` package `ellmer` [@wickham2026ellmer], from Posit, provides an R-native interface to LLM APIs: ```r install.packages("ellmer") library(ellmer) # pick a backend chat <- chat_claude(model = "claude-sonnet-4-5") # or chat_openai(), chat_gemini(), chat_ollama() for local # single turn chat$chat("Translate this regex to plain English: '^\\d{3}-\\d{2}-\\d{4}$'") # multi-turn keeps history chat$chat("What about variants with no separator?") # streaming chat$chat_async("Long analysis...", stream = TRUE) ``` Why programmatic access matters: - **Reproducibility.** A prompt in a script is versionable; a copy-paste from a chat window is not. - **Composition.** You can wrap an LLM call inside an R function: input from your data, output back to your pipeline. - **Tooling.** `ellmer` supports tool use (the LLM calls R functions you provide), structured output (JSON schema validation), and streaming. Set the API key once via environment variable: ```r # in .Renviron (project-local) ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... ``` Restart R; `ellmer` reads the env vars automatically. ## Claude Code and similar CLI agents For book-sized work or large refactors, an interactive CLI agent (Claude Code, GitHub Copilot CLI, Cursor) gives the LLM direct file-edit and shell-execution access. The agent can read files, make targeted edits, run tests, and iterate based on the output. When to reach for a CLI agent: - Multi-file refactors where the LLM needs to see the whole project structure. - Iterative debugging where the LLM needs to run the code and observe failures. - Large-scope tasks (write a chapter, set up a package) where copy-paste would be tedious. When not: - Quick lookups (use the chat window). - Tasks where you want full control of every edit (the agent is more autonomous than you may want). The CLI agent is more capable and more dangerous than a chat window. The verification step (reviewing every change before commit) is the safety mechanism. By 2026 the field has a name for the distinction that verification step marks. 'Vibe coding' is prompting an agent, accepting what it produces, and running it without reading the diff; it is a reasonable posture for a disposable script only you will use. 'Agentic coding' (or agentic engineering) is the same plan-write-execute-iterate loop with a human reviewing the diff against a real acceptance criterion before it is trusted. The two look identical from the terminal. They differ only in whether anyone checked. Everything in this chapter, and in the exercises that follow it, is written for the second posture. Treat the first as something you do only when being wrong costs nothing. ## LLM failure modes in R A non-exhaustive catalog of bugs that appear in LLM-generated R code: **Hallucinated functions.** The LLM produces `dplyr::mutate_groups()` (does not exist) or `tidyr::pivot_wider_with_progress()` (made up). Looks plausible; is not real. Run the code and a 'function not found' error catches it. **Silent type coercion.** The LLM uses `==` between a numeric and a character; R coerces; the comparison silently fails. Or the LLM compares a factor with a character; the comparison sometimes works, sometimes does not. **Wrong default in look-alike functions.** `t.test` in R defaults to Welch's correction; in some languages it does not. The LLM may assume the wrong default. Similarly, `cor` defaults to pairwise Pearson; LLM-trained code may assume something else. **Outdated APIs from training cut-off.** The LLM was trained before `dplyr 1.1.0`'s `relationship` argument; its joins lack the assertion. Or the LLM quotes the deprecated `dplyr::summarise_each` when the modern `across` would do. **Brittle regexes.** A regex that works on the example inputs but fails on plausible variants (international characters, leading whitespace, unusual punctuation). **Plausibly-wrong statistics.** The LLM uses a chi-square when Fisher's exact is needed for sparse tables. Or computes 'standard error' as the sample SD without the divide by `sqrt(n)`. These look right at the surface and require statistical review to catch. **`T` vs `TRUE`.** Some LLM-generated code uses `T` as a literal. `T` is a variable that defaults to `TRUE`, which means `T <- FALSE` later breaks the code. Best practice: always use the constants `TRUE` and `FALSE`. **Hybrid base/tidyverse.** A pipeline that mixes `dplyr::filter` and `stats::filter` (which is a time-series function with completely different semantics). The error message is unhelpful. **Untested edge cases.** The LLM produces code that works on the example you provided but breaks on NA, empty, single-row, or zero-variance input. ::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true} ## Check your understanding: catching a hallucinated API **Question.** The LLM produces: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} data <- data.frame(grp = c("a", "a", "b"), x = c(1, 3, 5)) data |> dplyr::summarise_groups(mean(x)) #> Error: #> ! 'summarise_groups' is not an exported object from 'namespace:dplyr' ``` ::: You run it and R cannot find the function. What is the right fix? **Answer.** The function does not exist. The LLM hallucinated it from `summarize` and `group_by`. The correct modern dplyr is: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} data |> dplyr::group_by(grp) |> dplyr::summarize(mean = mean(x)) #> # A tibble: 2 × 2 #> grp mean #> #> 1 a 2 #> 2 b 5 ``` ::: The LLM may also have meant `summarize(.by = grp, ...)` in newer dplyr. Verify against the package documentation rather than against another LLM suggestion. The general lesson: when an LLM- suggested function is unfamiliar, look it up in `?package::function` or on the package's CRAN page before trusting that it exists. The 'function not found' error is the cheapest catch; the harder catches are functions that exist but do something different from what the LLM thinks. ::: ## The verify-first workflow The workflow has one structural property worth naming before the steps: there is a gate, and generated code does not pass it by looking plausible. @fig-verify-loop is the loop, with the failure edge drawn in, because the failure edge is the part that gets skipped under deadline. ```{mermaid} %%| echo: false %%| label: fig-verify-loop %%| fig-alt: "Verification loop. A prompt yields generated code, %%| which is read end to end, run on the happy path, run on edge %%| cases including NA, empty input, a single row, wrong types and %%| zero variance, then compared against a reference such as a %%| closed form or your own version. A decision node asks whether %%| it is correct: no returns to the prompt, yes proceeds to %%| writing a test that locks the behavior, then committing." %%| fig-cap: "The verify-first loop. Plausibility is what the model %%| optimizes for and is not what you are checking. Every arrow %%| back to the prompt is a case the model got wrong in a way that %%| running the happy path alone would not have revealed." flowchart TD P["Prompt"] --> C["Generated code"] C --> R["Read end to end
can you say what it does?"] R --> H["Run the happy path"] H --> E["Run the edge cases
NA, empty, single row,
wrong type, zero variance"] E --> B["Compare to a reference
closed form, or your own version"] B --> G{"correct?"} G -->|"no"| P G -->|"yes"| T["Write a test
lock the behavior"] T --> M["Commit"] ``` Before committing any LLM-generated code: 1. **Read end-to-end.** Understand what the code is doing line by line. If you cannot, ask the LLM to explain (and then verify the explanation). 2. **Run on the happy path.** Confirm it produces the expected output for typical input. 3. **Run on edge cases.** NA, empty input, wrong type, single observation, all-zeros, all-NA. These are where bugs hide. 4. **Compare to a reference.** A known-good implementation, a closed-form solution, a simpler version you wrote yourself. 5. **Write a test.** Lock the behavior in testthat. Future regressions are caught automatically. 6. **Only then commit.** Skipping any step turns the LLM into a plausibility-generator rather than a correctness- generator. ## Readable code is auditable code The first step of that workflow, reading the code end to end, is only possible if the code is readable, and this is where consistent style stops being a matter of taste and becomes a matter of correctness. A diff you cannot read is a diff you cannot audit, and in the age of generated code the volume of diff to audit has gone up. Style is the tool that keeps the reading tractable. Adopt one style and impose it mechanically rather than by hand. The `tidyverse` style guide [@wickham2023style] is the de facto standard in applied R; two tools apply and enforce it: ```r # reformat a file or a project to the style guide styler::style_file("R/clean.R") styler::style_dir("R") # flag style and correctness lapses without changing the file lintr::lint("R/clean.R") lintr::lint_dir("R") ``` `styler` rewrites whitespace, indentation, and assignment to a canonical form. `lintr` is a static analyzer that flags what `styler` cannot fix, including some genuine bugs: a variable used before assignment, an `=` where `<-` was meant, the `T`/`TRUE` hazard from the failure-modes catalog above. Running `lintr` over LLM-generated code catches a useful fraction of the mechanical mistakes before you spend attention on the substantive ones. The reason this belongs in the AI chapter specifically: when you and a model produce code together, the model's output arrives in whatever style its training data averaged to, which is not necessarily yours. Passing it through `styler` on the way in normalizes it to the surrounding code, so that the diff a reviewer (or future-you) reads reflects what *changed* rather than whose keyboard it came from. The code-review checklist of @sec-git-teams assumes a readable diff; `styler` and `lintr` are how you guarantee one. Wire them into the continuous-integration workflow of @sec-ci and the guarantee holds for every contributor, human or not. ::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true} ## Check your understanding: the code that ran clean **Question.** An LLM writes a function. You read it, it looks right, you run it on your data and it returns plausible numbers with no errors or warnings. How much has that established? **Answer.** Almost nothing, and the reason is what makes LLM code a distinct problem rather than just more code to review. A language model is optimizing for plausibility. That is the objective, and it applies to the output as much as the source: code that looks like correct code, producing numbers that look like correct numbers. Your three checks tested readability, execution and plausibility, which are the three things the model is best at producing independently of correctness. What you have ruled out is syntax errors and hard crashes. What remains: silent type coercion, a look-alike function with a different default, an outdated API that still runs, an off-by-one in a filter, and a subtly wrong statistical choice that no amount of reading catches because it is defensible-looking. The verify-first loop exists because the happy path is the one case a plausible-looking wrong answer is most likely to survive. Edge cases (`NA`, empty input, a single row, zero variance) break plausible-but-wrong code where typical input does not, and comparison against a reference you computed independently is the only check that does not route through your own judgment about how the code looks. The generalization is uncomfortable and worth sitting with: your confidence after reading generated code is evidence about the code's *readability*, which the model optimized for, and not about its correctness, which it did not. ::: ## When not to reach for an LLM Tasks where the cognitive cost of evaluating the output exceeds the cost of writing it yourself: **Functions you have written many times.** A simple `mutate(age_group = cut(...))` is faster typed than prompted. The LLM round-trip costs more than the typing. **Code where correctness is hard to verify.** A complex regex on text you do not have full examples of. The LLM's output may be plausible but wrong on inputs you have not seen yet. **Domain-specific judgments.** Should you use multiple imputation or complete-case? Is this covariate a confounder? These depend on knowledge the LLM lacks. Solicit suggestions, but do not delegate the judgment. **Code you cannot afford to ship without understanding.** A function in your statistical inference code base that other people will rely on. Audit, test, and review with full understanding. An LLM multiplies what you already understand. It does not substitute for understanding you do not have. ## Prompt patterns that work A few patterns yield better results than free-form chat: **Specify the output shape.** 'Return a tibble with columns x, y, z.' Less ambiguity, fewer follow-up turns. **Provide examples.** 'Input: c("Aug 2024", "Sep 2024"). Output: c(2024-08-01, 2024-09-01)'. The LLM infers the rule. **Ask for tests.** 'Write the function and three tests covering happy path, NA input, and empty input.' Tests double as a specification check. **Demand explanation.** 'Write the function and explain in one paragraph why your implementation is correct.' If the explanation is shaky, the implementation is too. **Negative constraints.** 'Do not use a for loop. Do not use base R's `merge`.' Constrains the solution space. The 'Collaborating with an LLM' callouts elsewhere in this book follow this template: a prompt, what to watch for in the response, and how to verify. Use the same structure when you save your own prompts. ## Worked example: a short ellmer script ```r library(ellmer) # a function that takes an R function and returns a one-paragraph # explanation of what it does explain_function <- function(fn) { src <- deparse(fn) prompt <- paste0( "Explain in one paragraph what this R function does, ", "and identify any obvious bugs or edge cases it does not handle:\n\n", paste(src, collapse = "\n") ) chat <- chat_claude(model = "claude-sonnet-4-5") chat$chat(prompt) } # use it explain_function(function(x) { x |> filter(!is.na(value)) |> summarize(mean = mean(value)) }) ``` The function: takes another R function, asks Claude to explain it. Useful for code review of unfamiliar functions. The LLM's explanation is a starting point; verify against your own reading. ## Where this book stands This book was developed with extensive use of Claude Code (an Anthropic CLI agent). The exercise was deliberate: produce a usable book about statistical computing in the AI era while using AI tools to do so. Lessons from that experience appear throughout the 'Collaborating with an LLM' callouts. The honest accounting: roughly 70% of the prose was drafted with LLM assistance, all of it reviewed and edited. Roughly 30% of the code examples were generated; the rest were written by hand. Bugs caught: a steady stream, mostly variants of the failure modes cataloged above. The book exists because the LLM amplified the author's writing throughput. The book is correct (to the extent it is) because the author verified every claim. The combination is what worked. Either alone would have been worse. ## Principle in use Three habits keep the model an amplifier: 1. **Verify before trusting.** Read end-to-end, run on edge cases, compare to a reference, test. 2. **Use the LLM as an amplifier.** Domain knowledge and substantive judgment remain the analyst's. The LLM accelerates routine work. 3. **Document the prompt.** A working prompt is a reusable specification. Save it in comments alongside the code, in a project-level prompts library, or as a 'Collaborating with an LLM' callout in your documentation. ## Exercises **On your own machine, data, or collaborations.** These exercises need API credentials and code of your own, so no answer key is possible. Each states what a good answer establishes. 1. Install `ellmer`. Write a short R function that uses `chat_claude()` to summarize a block of code you paste in. Keep the function under 20 lines. 2. Pick a function from an earlier chapter and ask an LLM to rewrite it. Score the rewrite against: correctness, style, test coverage, documentation. Decide whether to adopt the rewrite and why. 3. Find an instance in your own recent code where an LLM gave you working-looking but wrong code. Write up the failure mode as a one-page case study for your research group. 4. Use an LLM to generate five adversarial inputs that break a function you wrote. Keep the ones that actually break. Write tests for them. 5. Set up Claude Code or a similar CLI agent. Use it to refactor a small project; document one bug it introduced and one improvement it made. ## Further reading - [@wickham2026ellmer], the R-native interface to LLMs used throughout this chapter. - Anthropic Claude Code documentation at `docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code`, the CLI agent used to develop this book. - [@huyen2024ai], *AI Engineering*, patterns for production LLM applications. - [@wickham2023style], the style guide worth imposing on generated code, since a diff you cannot read is a diff you cannot audit. ## Prerequisites answers {#sec-quiz-answers-21} 1. `ellmer` provides a standard R interface to multiple LLM backends (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, etc.) with multi-turn history, streaming output, and tool-calling support. It lets you invoke the model from scripts, parameterize prompts with R values, and build a programmatic layer over what would otherwise be manual copy-paste. A browser chatbot is interactive only and produces no reproducible artifact. 2. (Any three of:) hallucinated APIs (calling functions or arguments that do not exist), silent type coercions that change results subtly, misuse of functions whose defaults differ from their names (e.g., `t.test()` defaults to Welch's correction), brittle regexes that look right but miss edge cases, hybrid base/tidyverse code that conflicts (`filter` from base vs `dplyr`), and pasting outdated package APIs from the model's training cut-off. 3. Writing the first draft yourself forces you to understand the problem. Without that understanding, you cannot evaluate the LLM's proposal: you will accept plausible-looking code whose bugs you cannot see. With it, you can judge the LLM's suggestion on its merits and spot the small differences that matter. The habit is the single biggest determinant of whether AI assistance produces correct work or plausible-looking work.
